subject: Modern History
sub_topic: Women in Civil Disobedience Movement — salt march participation

concepts.name: Gandhi's Deliberate Exclusion and Subsequent Inclusion of Women in the Salt March
key_dimensions: Gandhi's initial reasoning for excluding women from the Dandi March (fear of trivializing the movement)
Sarojini Naidu's role in persuading Gandhi to allow women's participation
The ideological tension between Gandhi's paternalistic protectiveness and women's agency
How this reversal set a precedent for women's mass mobilization in CDM

concepts.name: Sarojini Naidu's Leadership at Dharasana Salt Works Raid (1930)
key_dimensions: Context: Gandhi's arrest before the planned raid and Naidu stepping in as leader
Webb Miller's eyewitness dispatch and its international propaganda impact
Naidu's symbolic role vs. operational command — distinction between figurehead and organizer
UPSC trap: Often confused with the Dandi March itself — Dharasana was a separate subsequent action

concepts.name: Kamladevi Chattopadhyay and the Commercialization of Civil Disobedience
key_dimensions: Her act of publicly selling illegal salt on the streets of Bombay as a political statement
Distinction from salt manufacturing — selling vs. producing contraband salt as forms of resistance
Her broader role in linking the CDM to economic nationalism and cottage industries
UPSC trap: Kamladevi is often confused with Kasturba Gandhi in mass mobilization narratives

concepts.name: Avantikabai Gokhale and the Organized Women's Picketing of Liquor Shops
key_dimensions: How liquor shop picketing became a parallel women's front to the salt satyagraha
The socio-economic logic: liquor prohibition linked to family welfare, making it a 'women's issue'
Gandhi's strategic framing of this as acceptable women's activism without physical danger
UPSC angle: Whether picketing constituted 'civil disobedience' proper or a separate allied movement

concepts.name: The 'Purdah Barrier' and Its Partial Breakdown During CDM
key_dimensions: How the CDM was the first mass movement to draw out women from purdah-observing communities at scale
Gandhi's deliberate appeal to domestic/motherhood metaphors to make public protest culturally acceptable
Geographic variation — purdah breakdown more visible in cities than rural areas
UPSC trap: CDM is often overstated as a complete rupture; scholars note its limits for Muslim women in purdah

concepts.name: Kasturba Gandhi's Symbolic and Organizational Role in CDM
key_dimensions: Her role as mobilizer of women in Gujarat and Sabarmati Ashram network
The 'wife of the Mahatma' effect — how her participation legitimized women's involvement for conservative families
Distinction between Kasturba's role in CDM vs. Quit India Movement (her most prominent independent role)
UPSC trap: Her arrest and imprisonment were more significant in Quit India (1942), not CDM — timeline confusion

concepts.name: Class and Caste Composition of Women Participants in the Salt March
key_dimensions: Predominantly upper-caste, educated, urban women in leadership vs. rural/lower-caste women as foot soldiers
Why Dalit women's participation was structurally limited — Ambedkar's critique of Congress mobilization
The 'nationalist woman' as a predominantly bhadramahila (respectable middle-class) construct
UPSC angle: This class skew is used to critique the CDM's claim of being a 'mass' women's movement

concepts.name: Mithuben Petit and the Bardoli Women's Movement as a CDM Precursor
key_dimensions: Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) as a training ground for women organizers who later joined CDM
Petit's organizational model: door-to-door mobilization in villages by women volunteers
How Bardoli established the template of women managing domestic non-cooperation (boycott of British goods)
UPSC trap: Bardoli is pre-CDM but its women's network directly fed into 1930 participation — often treated as unrelated

concepts.name: Women's Volunteer Corps (Desh Sewika Sangh) and Institutional Organization
key_dimensions: Formation of parallel women's volunteer units to coordinate with the Congress machinery during CDM
Functions: picketing, propaganda, relief for arrested families, maintaining supply chains for satyagrahis
The tension between these bodies and mainstream Congress committees over autonomy and recognition
UPSC angle: These bodies represent proto-feminist organizational structures within a nationalist framework

concepts.name: The Role of Women in Manufacturing and Distributing Contraband Salt
key_dimensions: Women boiling seawater and salt-making in coastal villages as a domestic act of defiance
Why this was harder for colonial police to suppress than male-led processions — the 'domestic space' advantage
Instances from coastal Tamil Nadu, Andhra, and Maharashtra where women dominated local salt production
UPSC trap: Salt production by women is often overlooked in favor of dramatic march narratives

concepts.name: British Colonial Response to Women Protestors: Policy of Restraint and Its Contradictions
key_dimensions: Initial British policy of not arresting women to avoid adverse publicity
How the Congress strategically deployed women in front lines, exploiting this hesitation
The eventual shift — mass arrests of women by mid-1930 and the government's dilemma
UPSC angle: This dynamic reveals how gender norms were instrumentalized by both nationalists and colonizers

concepts.name: International Propaganda Value of Women's Participation in CDM
key_dimensions: Foreign press coverage (Webb Miller, American journalists) emphasizing non-violent women facing lathi charges
How images of women satyagrahis shaped international opinion against British rule
Eleanor Roosevelt and American women's organizations expressing solidarity — diplomatic dimension
UPSC angle: The propaganda function distinguishes CDM women's participation from earlier movements in scale and intent

concepts.name: Gandhi's Ideological Framework for Women's Participation: Shakti vs. Feminist Agency
key_dimensions: Gandhi's view of women as naturally suited for satyagraha due to innate suffering and self-sacrifice
The tension between his 'shakti' rhetoric (empowering) and its implicit reinforcement of traditional gender roles
How feminist historians (Madhu Kishwar, Geraldine Forbes) critique Gandhi's mobilization as instrumental
UPSC trap: Portraying Gandhi's approach as straightforwardly feminist vs. the more nuanced scholarly critique

concepts.name: Regional Variation in Women's Participation: Tamil Nadu, Bengal, and Gujarat Compared
key_dimensions: Gujarat: Brahmin and Patidar women's networks — organized, caste-based, linked to Gandhi's home base
Tamil Nadu: C. Rajagopalachari's Vedaranyam March and women's participation in coastal salt satyagraha
Bengal: Presence of revolutionary nationalist women (Pritilata Waddedar) vs. Gandhian non-violent women — ideological split
UPSC trap: Conflating Bengal's armed revolutionary women with CDM participants — they operated in parallel, not together

concepts.name: Pritilata Waddedar and the Intersection of Armed Nationalism and the CDM Period
key_dimensions: Waddedar's 1932 Chittagong Armory Raid participation — contemporaneous with but distinct from CDM
Why she is significant: represents the non-Gandhian path of women's nationalism during the same historical moment
Her death (self-administered cyanide) as a martyrdom narrative in Bengali nationalism
UPSC trap: She is frequently misplaced within CDM — she was a revolutionary, not a civil disobedience participant

concepts.name: Post-CDM Political Outcomes for Women: Congress Representation and Institutional Gains
key_dimensions: Whether CDM participation translated into increased representation in Congress committees
The 1931 Karachi Resolution and women's rights provisions — link to women's CDM contribution
Gap between symbolic recognition of women's sacrifice and actual political empowerment within Congress
UPSC angle: The CDM as both a high point and a missed opportunity for institutionalizing women's political gains

concepts.name: Hansa Mehta and Renuka Ray: Educated Urban Women Bridging CDM and Constitutional Nationalism
key_dimensions: Their CDM participation as a stepping stone to later roles in the Constituent Assembly
How their nationalist credentials from CDM gave legitimacy to their demands for gender equality in the Constitution
Distinction: they represented the English-educated elite stream, not grassroots mobilization
UPSC angle: Direct line from CDM activism to Article 15(3) and women's rights provisions in Constitution

concepts.name: The CDM and Muslim Women's Participation: The Communal Fault Line
key_dimensions: Limited Muslim women's participation due to purdah norms and the Muslim League's non-cooperation with CDM
Exceptions: some Muslim women in Congress-aligned families in UP and Bihar
How this gap was later used in Two-Nation Theory rhetoric — Congress as a 'Hindu' movement
UPSC trap: The CDM is often presented as a pan-Indian women's movement; the Muslim women's absence is a critical nuance

concepts.name: Newspaper 'Young India', 'Harijan', and the Media Construction of the 'Nationalist Woman'
key_dimensions: Gandhi's writings constructing the ideal woman satyagrahi — domestic virtues + public courage
How Congress-aligned press coverage of women's participation shaped public memory and mythology
The selective amplification of upper-caste women's stories over anonymous rural/Dalit women participants
UPSC angle: Media and memory construction is a historiographical concept increasingly tested in Mains

concepts.name: CDM Women's Participation vs. Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22): Comparative Escalation
key_dimensions: Scale comparison: CDM saw significantly larger and more organized women's participation than NCM
Structural reason: Gandhi's specific call to women in 1930 vs. implicit inclusion in 1920
Qualitative shift: From supporting roles (spinning, boycott) in NCM to frontline satyagraha in CDM
UPSC trap: Treating NCM and CDM women's roles as equivalent — CDM represents a qualitative escalation, not mere continuity
